extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of natural philosophy (physics, astronomy, geology, biology, psychology)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Herbert Spencer's cross-disciplinary principles about how motion is directed in physical, organic, mental, and social systems — principally the idea that motion follows lines of least resistance or the resultant of opposing forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universally co-existent forces as symbolic constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: The attractive and repulsive forces we conceive are not absolute realities but 'our symbols of the reality' — forms under which the Unknowable is cognizable; useful though not absolutely true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the conceptual forces of attraction and repulsion as idealized, relatively true constructs used to interpret phenomena when direct tactual experience is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resultant-of-forces law of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Movement takes place along the resultant of all tractions (attractive forces) and resistances (repulsive forces); strictly speaking this resultant law is the sole law of direction of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing any motion, consider the vector sum (resultant) of all attractive and repulsive influences rather than only one dominant force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line of greatest traction and line of least resistance as practical approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where attractive forces alone are appreciable, movement follows the line of greatest traction; where repulsive forces alone are appreciable, movement follows the line of least resistance; these are often acceptable approximations when one kind of force vastly predominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'greatest traction' or 'least resistance' approximations for practical problems when one class of force is overwhelmingly dominant (e.g., falling bodies, escaping steam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Momentum and the continuation of motion (inertia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Movement set up in any direction is itself a cause of further movement in that direction because it embodies a surplus force (expressed in the law of inertia for motion through space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the sustaining effect of existing motion (momentum) when predicting subsequent motion — applies to transit through space, through matter, and propagation of vibrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbability of perfectly straight motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The direction of motion can rarely if ever be perfectly straight because forces of attraction and repulsion must be symmetrically disposed around the path for absolute straightness — a condition extremely unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect curvature/indirectness in real motion due to unsymmetrical distributions of surrounding forces; perfect straight lines are idealizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity of path increases with number and variety of forces
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion as the forces at work are numerous and varied, the curve a moving body describes is necessarily more complex (e.g., contrast arrow flight vs. a stick tossed by breakers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple interactions are present, model the trajectory as a complex, possibly three-dimensional curve with time-varying equation rather than simple conic sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nebular condensation and emergent rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: In nebular condensation, flocculi moving toward a common centre under unsymmetrical forms have resultants that are curved and, by composition of forces among many such flocculi, a rotation of the whole nebula in one direction results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply resultant-of-forces reasoning to early nebular aggregation to explain emergent rotation of astrophysical systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planetary and satellite motion as resultant of tangential momentum and centripetal forces, with perturbations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each planet's momentum (tending to carry it tangent) and centripetal gravitation (toward primary) combine to produce the observed curve; adjacent bodies cause perturbations producing deviations from exact circles/ellipses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tangential momentum, central attraction, and time-varying perturbing influences when modeling planetary motion; predict small divergences (perturbations) from ideal two-body orbits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric currents follow resultants of tractive forces and variable resistances
rubrics_metrics.description: Heated air expands, reducing lateral resistance and causing flows toward regions of lessened resistance; throughout each generated current the direction is the resultant of Earth's tractive force and resistance offered by surrounding air, modified by other currents and collisions with crustal prominences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining winds and large-scale atmospheric motion, consider local heating, pressure gradients (resistance changes), Earth's gravity, and interactions with other currents and topography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaporation and condensation as motions governed by resistance differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaporation is escape of water particles in the direction of least resistance (diminished mutual pressure); condensation arises when mutual pressure among condensing particles diminishes causing motion toward lessened resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret phase-change-driven flows (evaporation/condensation) mechanically as particle motions responding to changing resistances/pressures in the medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrological flows and stream paths as resultants of gravity and local resistances
rubrics_metrics.description: The path of raindrops and streams is determined by Earth's attraction and the resistance of atmospheric currents or surrounding solids; cascades exemplify combined gravity and horizontal momentum producing parabolic trajectories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model water-course trajectories using combined effects of gravity, local resistances (channel morphology), and existing momentum; expect three-dimensional, variable equations for ocean and river flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological/igneous phenomena tend to expend along lines of least resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Although direct inductive proof is limited, observed facts (earthquakes revisiting same localities, volcanoes distributed along lines and recurring vents) imply that igneous/tectonic forces expend along previously-fractured lines of least resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the least-resistance principle as a working hypothesis to explain repeated seismic activity and volcanic venting patterns tied to pre-existing crustal fractures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic growth proceeds along lines of least resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Organic form results from motion, and motion takes the direction of least resistance; examples include root growth insinuating through soil interstices and spiral tendencies in growth due to motion under resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain shapes of plant roots, leaf arrangements, and many spiral forms as outcomes of incremental growth following paths of least mechanical resistance combined with local availability of nutritive materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiral form as indicator of motion under resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion under resistance tends to take a spiral direction (e.g., bubbles rising in water, falling bodies in viscous media), offering a prima facie case for the prevalence of spiral forms in organic bodies (branches, leaves, heart development).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering spiral organic structures, consider hydrodynamic/mechanical analogies (motion + resistance) as explanatory mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gravity and tractive forces significantly modify organic shapes
rubrics_metrics.description: In organic growth, tractive forces (gravity) materially affect direction of branches, flowers, and leaves; thus the 'least resistance' formula is incomplete without including such tractive forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include gravitational effects when applying least-resistance reasoning to organismal morphology; expected deviations from purely resistance-driven forms will occur due to weight and cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological functions (circulation, secretions) follow channels of least resistance and are affected by gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Vessels for blood, lymph, bile, etc., are channels of least resistance; currents along them are altered by Earth's tractive force (evidence: varicose veins, relief of inflammation by elevation, positional oedema changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret circulatory/lymphatic flow patterns and positional clinical signs in terms of flow along paths of least resistance modulated by gravitational forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection and species development as structural change along lines of least resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: From a dynamic view, natural selection implies structural changes along lines where antagonistic forces are least; multiplication and preservation of varieties occur where antagonistic forces are smaller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'least resistance' as a heuristic for understanding why populations flourish and morphologically adapt in particular localities; local environmental antagonisms shape selection trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nervous processes and sensations interpreted as motion along least-resistance neural channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Though not outwardly visible, sensations and volitions imply motions propagated through the organism along channels that, through repeated discharge, offer least resistance; a sensation adds force at one point and motion flows toward parts where force is expended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model neural excitation and propagation as flows seeking paths of least resistance, with repeated use lowering resistance and strengthening the path (habit formation, reflex arcs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of habitual/reflex pathways by reduction of resistance through repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated motion between two points diminishes resistance along the channel (through reaction upon traversed tissues), leading to permanent lines of communication — explaining reflex action and stable nervous connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for habit and reflex formation by treating repeated neural/muscular discharge as a mechanism that reduces obstruction and biases future flows along the same routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of muscular excitation under emotion follows least-resistance channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Undirected emotional discharges affect first muscles that are small and frequently acted on (least resistance), then progressively larger muscles as intensity increases (e.g., laughter sequence: mouth muscles -> vocal/respiratory -> limbs -> spine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predict the sequence of involuntary muscular involvement under affective states by identifying muscles with lower resistive thresholds due to frequent use or small mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volitions and deliberate actions are incipient discharges along previously established least-resistance lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A volition represents the movements intended and partially excites associated motor nerves; previous experiences render certain channels lines of least resistance, so volition completes a discharge along these paths — thereby achieving ends with minimal total force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing choice of actions, consider that individuals tend to choose routes requiring the smallest expenditure of force relative to their own knowledge and neural conditioning; ignorance or lack of skill creates effective obstacles that change which path is 'least resistance' for that agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/societal growth follows directions of least average opposing forces
rubrics_metrics.description: As societies are composite organisms, their growth and spread follow directions where the average of antagonistic forces (climate, food availability, predators, competing peoples, costs of maintaining heat) is smallest; population spreads toward fertile valleys, seashores, and tropical regions where survival costs are lower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the least-resistance principle to migration, colonization, and the geographic origins of large societies: expect human populations to concentrate where net antagonisms to self-preservation are minimized.
